summary: For ages 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): how minibeasts move (crawling, flying, slithering, jumping, burrowing, swimming) and the body features that go with each movement, with leg-counting (ant 6, spider 8, woodlouse many, worm/snail none) as a first concrete grouping cue. The core aim is form-to-function reasoning at a simple level: wings let a creature fly, strong back legs let it jump, no legs plus muscles let it slither. Children observe real movement, act it out, count legs, sort by way of moving, and record simple movement/leg data.
misconceptions: 'All minibeasts crawl / move the same way' — missing the variety of movement.
'Spiders and insects are the same' — leg count (8 vs 6) is the first cue that they differ.
'Worms and snails have tiny legs' — children assume all creatures have legs; some move by muscle/foot.
'Movement isn't connected to body shape' — not yet linking wings/legs to how a creature moves.
Miscounting legs by counting antennae or by not counting both sides.

activities.title: Sort minibeasts by how they move, then count their legs
steps: Watch each minibeast actually move — through slow-motion video, real observation, or an animation that plays when the creature is tapped (a grasshopper springs, a worm ripples and burrows, a bee lifts off).

Sort each creature into a way-of-moving bin by its main or most noticeable way of moving: flies / crawls / slithers / jumps / burrows / swims. Talk about creatures that move in more than one way (a grasshopper jumps but can also crawl and fly; an earthworm slithers on the surface and burrows underground; a bee flies but also crawls).

Count the legs on an ant (6) and a spider (8) by touching or tapping each leg one at a time and counting aloud; count both sides of the body so none are missed, and count only the walking legs — on the ant, do not count the two feelers (antennae) at the head as legs.
Place the ant and spider into different leg-number groups, and place worms/snails in a 'no legs' group.
Record the result as a simple tally or pictogram of how many legs each creature has.
activities.insight: Minibeasts move in different ways, and leg number (6 vs 8 vs many vs none) is a concrete, countable way to begin grouping them — foreshadowing later 'is it an insect?' work.

activities.title: Match the body feature to the movement
steps: Match a body-feature card to the creature and movement it enables: wings → fly (bee, butterfly), strong back legs → jump (grasshopper), many legs → crawl, no legs + muscles → slither.

Where an interactive picture is available, drag the feature onto the creature and watch the picture respond — give the grasshopper its big back legs and it can jump; remove the bee's wings and it can no longer fly.
Say or complete a reason sentence: 'Grasshoppers have big back legs SO they can jump'; 'Worms have no legs so they move by squeezing and stretching.'
activities.insight: How a minibeast moves comes from the body parts it has — the first form-to-function reasoning children do.

activities.title: Three minibeasts: count and explain (diagnostic)
steps: Look at an ant, a spider, and an earthworm. Say how many legs each one has (6, 8, and 0).
Explain how the one with no legs gets around — the worm squeezes and stretches its body, its muscles pushing it along and tiny bristles gripping the soil.
Extend to a new case: predict whether a snail has legs and how it moves (it has no legs and glides on a muscular foot over slime — a different legless mechanism from the worm).
Consider a probe: 'A centipede — would you expect 6 legs, 8, or lots more? Why?' and 'If something has 6 legs, what might it be?'
activities.insight: Leg number and way of moving are connected, not memorised as separate facts; some creatures move with no legs at all, and different legless creatures (worm vs snail) can move differently.

checkQuestion: Here are three minibeasts: an ant, a spider, and an earthworm. How many legs does each one have? And how does the one with no legs get around?
checkAnswer: An ant has 6 legs, a spider has 8 legs, and an earthworm has 0 legs. The worm has no legs at all — it moves by squeezing and stretching its body (its muscles push it along, and tiny bristles grip the soil). Different minibeasts move in different ways: walking on legs, crawling, or wriggling.
